title: Nora Fatehi Just Took the Stage at the World Cup. Bollywood Has Never Had This Kind of Night.
excerpt: The Canadian-born Bollywood star performed 'Siir Siir' at Toronto's opening ceremony alongside Michael Bublé and Alanis Morissette — and reminded a billion viewers why she's one of the most magnetic performers on the planet.
body:
The sun was still high over Toronto's BMO Field on Friday afternoon when Nora Fatehi walked onto the biggest stage in sport and did what she does best: stopped the room.

The 2026 FIFA World Cup's Canadian opening ceremony — the second of three across Mexico, Canada, and the United States — was designed to announce a country to the world. It opened with Indigenous drummers and a welcome from William Prince. Alessia Cara emerged from behind a gilded golden ball to belt out Wild Things. Michael Bublé crooned Sam Cooke's Bring It On Home to Me with the easy warmth of a man who's been serenading stadiums for two decades. Alanis Morissette closed it all with O Canada, her voice enormous against a pitch draped in crimson.

And somewhere in the middle of all that Canadian star power, Nora Fatehi and French artist Vegedream took the stage and performed 'Siir Siir' — an official 2026 World Cup anthem rooted in a Moroccan fan chant that went viral during Qatar 2022. The song is intoxicating: part North African folk rhythm, part global pop anthem, the kind of track that doesn't need subtitles to move a stadium. And Fatehi, who has built an entire career on exactly that kind of energy, owned every second of it.

This is not her first time on the World Cup stage. In 2022, Fatehi performed at the FIFA Fan Festival in Qatar, where her appearance cemented her status as one of the few Bollywood-adjacent artists with genuine global crossover pull. But performing at the opening ceremony — alongside Bublé, Morissette, Jessie Reyez, and Elyanna — is a different tier entirely. This is the broadcast that over a billion people tune into. This is the lineup that sits next to Shakira's Mexico City spectacle the night before and Katy Perry's Los Angeles blowout later that evening.

For the Indian diaspora, the moment carries a particular resonance. Nora Fatehi was born in Toronto to a family of Moroccan descent. She moved to India as a young woman and built her career from the ground up in Bollywood — first as a dancer, then as a singer, then as a full-blown multimedia star. Her trajectory is, in a way, a reverse-NRI story: instead of leaving India for the West, she left the West for India, and India embraced her completely. Songs like Dilbar, O Saki Saki, and Kusu Kusu turned her into one of the most-watched performers in Hindi cinema. Her Instagram following — north of 50 million — puts her in the same conversation as mainstream Western pop stars.

"The opening ceremony in Toronto will be a powerful reflection of Canada's identity." — FIFA President Gianni Infantino

And now she's back in Toronto, performing on home soil, on a stage that makes Filmfare look like a neighbourhood talent show. The symmetry is almost too perfect: the girl who left Canada for Bollywood returning as a FIFA-endorsed global artist to the city where it all began.

The broader picture matters too. The 2026 World Cup has three opening ceremonies — one for each host nation. Mexico City got Shakira and Burna Boy performing Dai Dai, the tournament's lead anthem, alongside J Balvin, Danny Ocean, Maná, and Tyla singing South Africa's national anthem. The United States ceremony, held later Friday at SoFi Stadium in Los Angeles, features Katy Perry, Future, Anitta, LISA, Rema, and Tyla again. And the grand finale? The World Cup final halftime show on July 19 will reportedly feature Madonna, Shakira, and BTS — yes, all three together.

Nora Fatehi sharing a lineup card with Bublé and Morissette puts her in rarified company for any Indian or Indian-adjacent performer. The last time Bollywood had this kind of representation at a FIFA event, it was Fatehi herself in Qatar. Before that, it was decades of the Indian entertainment industry watching from the sidelines while Latin, African, and K-Pop acts dominated the global sporting stage.

For NRIs watching from the couch in New Jersey or Mississauga, this was the rare moment where two parts of your identity — the country you live in and the culture you stream — collided on the same stage, at the same time, in front of the entire world.

The ceremony gave way to the match: Canada drew Bosnia and Herzegovina 1-1 in their first-ever home World Cup game. Cyle Larin scored for Canada. The stadium shook.

But the image that will last isn't a goal. It's Nora Fatehi, standing on the pitch at BMO Field in Toronto, performing a Moroccan-inspired World Cup anthem for a global audience of over a billion — Bollywood's most electrifying dancer, back where she started, bigger than she's ever been.
